You'd be the average person. Basically, would you rather be from an ordinary American family 100 years ago or an ordinary Ethiopian family today?

Because conditions 100 years ago just weren't that bad if you were in a rich country. People had good food, comfortable housing and a relatively reasonable work load. One male worker could support a multi-generational family; wife, kids and declining parents. They also had access to a family doctor who gave them reasonable care in accordance with the medical knowledge of the time. It was only 25 years before penicillin came into popular use in 1940 so you had a good chance of benefiting from that. And, in the 1930's there was sulfa in use as an antibiotic. Education was available and arguably better than today. Also, crime was less of an issue with many people not even having locks on their doors, not feeling there was a need for any. Barring death, families generally stayed intact. It certainly was not utopia by any stretch of the imagination. Women were pretty much under the rule of their husbands and opportunity was far from anything approaching equal for all but for the very vast majority it beat the hell out of poor countries today.

Blood and Sand (The original recipe from 1930):

  • .75 oz The Glenrothes Select Reserve Single Malt Scotch Whisky

  • .75 oz Sweet vermouth

  • .75 oz Cherry Heering

  • .75 oz Orange Juice

Add all the ingredients to a shaker and fill with ice. Shake, and strain into a chilled coupe or cocktail glass. Garnish with an orange peel.

Now for mixed drinks I got three for you:

Caipirinha is a very light, but very alcoholic, summer Brazilian drink. It's essentially brown sugar and lime crushed together with Cachaça. This stuff goes down too easy.

Sazerac is the official drink of New Orleans and the oldest mixed drink. It has absinthe, cognac, bitters, and usually garnished with a lemon peel.

Boston Sour is essentially a Whiskey Sour made with an egg white and garnished with bitters. I've had my bartender friend argue with me that once upon a time this was the 'real' way to make a whiskey sour but I don't know how true this is.
